191 years ago, January 23, 1828, the last rebellious Samurai leader, Saigō Takamori, is born in Satsuma, Japan.

Saigō was born into a lower class of Samurai in the Japanese caste system. During this time period Japan began to industrialize their nation and modernize it with political changes inspired by European nations. The Meiji Restoration Imperial Government restored monarchy and abolished the caste system that placed the Samurai on top, causing many of them to rebel against the new government in The Boshin War.

Always loyal to the new Emperor, Saigō trained and bravely led Imperial troops against the many Samurai factions that rebelled against him. Disagreements amongst the political class would inspire Saigō to retire from politics and seek a peaceful life as a military instructor. However the new modernized government became concerned with Saigō influence amongst thousands of warriors and sent undercover agents to spy on him. When Saigō’s fiercely loyal students discovered the government agents, they tortured and killed many of them thinking they were assassins.

Saigō had no desire for a war against the Emperor and put on his old Imperial Uniform to go visit Tokyo and deescalate the situation. But one of the worst winters in Japanese history prevented his travel and many of the Samurai took it as an omen to rebel. Saigō was asked to lead the rebellion against the government, a task he reluctantly accepted. Thousands of veteran warriors and young students flocked to the noble warrior’s side.

The Samurai took the initiative and placed a government stronghold under siege in their territory. The government in response sent over 90,000 troops to face off against the rebel’s 15,000. After nearly 2 weeks of fighting and heavy losses, Saigō called off the siege and retreated around the island, leaving behind small numbers of rebel groups to engage in guerrilla warfare. Saigō continually escaped and out maneuvered the government troops for months until his force was severely diminished.

Understanding the end was near, Saigō burned his personal belongings and Imperial uniform he wore loyally for many years and during the early stages of the rebellion. The rebels were down to around 500 warriors and they took their final position on top of a fortified mountain. Not wanting to take any chances, the Imperial government encircled this mountain with 30,000 soldiers and 5 modern warships making sure no escape was possible. Leading the government troops was Saigō’s old military friend, Yamagata Aritomo. Surrounding and outnumbering his foe 60 to 1, Yamagata had no desire to kill him and pleaded with his old companion to surrender and avoid further effusion of blood. The rebels had the night of September 23rd to make their choice as the final assault would begin the next morning.

Bushido code forbade surrender and Saigō spent his last night on earth partaking in a sake party with his rebel soldiers. The assault opened with a large artillery barrage and gunfire was exchanged between both sides as the Imperial infantry moved up the mountain onto the rebel positions. In an iconic fight scene, ~1000 year old swordsmanship went against 19th century soldiers in close quarters melee combat. The government conscripts suffered some causalities but were eventually able to overrun the small numbers of Samurai and pick them apart with rifles. Saigō Takamori was wounded and his final moments are still disputed with either him committing seppuku or having a friend assist him with his death.

Now leaderless and nearly all their comrades killed, the last surviving 40 Samurai adhered to tradition and refused to surrender. Until dawn they held on and then with swords drawn they rushed down the mountain and were shot by the government troops. The feudal warrior class that had ruled Japan for centuries went out in a blaze and faded into history being defeated by foreign-made modern weaponry wielded by lower-class soldiers they despised.
